drafted_by: AI, requires clinician review before any real use.

questions.text: What is the main breast problem: a lump, pain, nipple discharge, skin change, swelling, or something else?
questions.rationale: Clarifying the main breast complaint guides the next branch of the interview.

questions.text: When did you first notice it, and has it changed?
questions.rationale: A new or changing finding is more concerning than long-stable cyclical pain.

questions.text: Where is the lump, about how big is it, and is it hard, mobile, or fixed?
questions.rationale: Mass character and location start the breast-cancer versus cyst assessment.

questions.text: Is the lump growing, and is there one lump or several?
questions.rationale: A growing dominant mass needs prompt imaging.

questions.text: Is there breast pain, is it one side, and does it change with your period?
questions.rationale: Cyclical bilateral pain is often benign; focal noncyclical pain needs evaluation.

questions.text: Is the skin dimpled, thickened like orange peel, red, or ulcerated?
questions.rationale: Peau d'orange, ulceration, or inflammatory changes raise concern for cancer or infection.

questions.text: Is there nipple discharge, and is it bloody, clear, or milky, and from one duct or many?
questions.rationale: Unilateral bloody or clear discharge is more concerning than bilateral milky discharge.

questions.text: Has the nipple pulled in, crusted, or changed shape?
questions.rationale: New inversion or eczema-like nipple change can indicate cancer or Paget disease.

questions.text: Is the breast red, hot, swollen, and painful, and have you had fever?
questions.rationale: This pattern suggests mastitis or abscess, and also inflammatory breast cancer.

questions.text: Have you felt lumps in the armpit or above the collarbone?
questions.rationale: Regional nodes change urgency of a breast finding.

questions.text: Is it one breast or both?
questions.rationale: Unilateral findings are more concerning than symmetric changes.

questions.text: Are you still having periods, on hormones or contraception, or pregnant or breastfeeding?
questions.rationale: Hormonal state changes the meaning of lumps, pain, and discharge.

questions.text: Did you injure the breast recently?
questions.rationale: Trauma can cause fat necrosis that mimics a mass.

questions.text: Has anyone in your family had breast, ovarian, or related cancers, especially at a young age?
questions.rationale: Family history and possible BRCA-related cancers change risk.

questions.text: Have you had breast cancer, radiation to the chest, or a prior abnormal biopsy?
questions.rationale: Personal history is the strongest risk factor for a new breast problem.

questions.text: When was your last mammogram or breast imaging, and were any findings followed up?
questions.rationale: Screening history avoids duplicate work and catches missed follow-up.

questions.text: Any unintended weight loss, bone pain, or new persistent cough or headache?
questions.rationale: These symptoms raise concern for advanced disease.

questions.text: Do you have breast implants, and any swelling, pain, or change in shape of the implant?
questions.rationale: Implant complications include rupture and rare associated lymphoma.

questions.text: Are you taking hormones, antipsychotics, or other medicines that can cause milky discharge?
questions.rationale: Medications commonly cause galactorrhea.

questions.text: Do you check your breasts, and is this different from what you usually feel?
questions.rationale: Patient-detected change is a common presentation.

questions.text: Have you had a prior breast biopsy, dense breasts, or been told you are at higher risk?
questions.rationale: Prior atypia and density change screening and workup intensity.

questions.text: Do you drink alcohol regularly, or have you used hormone replacement for a long time?
questions.rationale: Alcohol and prolonged estrogen exposure modestly raise breast cancer risk.

questions.text: How much is the pain or worry affecting sleep and daily life?
questions.rationale: Impact and distress guide support while workup proceeds.

questions.text: What is the main thing you are worried this could be?
questions.rationale: Understanding the patient's concern guides reassurance and follow-up questions.

red_flags.label: Growing or hard breast lump
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe a new, hard, or growing breast lump?

red_flags.label: Skin dimpling, orange-peel change, or ulceration
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report dimpled, thickened, red, or ulcerated breast skin?

red_flags.label: New nipple inversion or bloody discharge
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report a nipple pulling in, crusting, or bloody discharge from one nipple?

red_flags.label: Red hot swollen breast with fever
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report a red, hot, swollen breast with fever?

red_flags.label: Breast finding with armpit or collarbone lumps
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report a breast lump together with lumps in the armpit or above the collarbone?

red_flags.label: Breast complaint with weight loss or bone pain
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report a breast problem together with weight loss, bone pain, or persistent cough?
